subtitle: Journal-club style ICU update: PICO, key results, appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English.

script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for October 19, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 3 - Preterm Risk Factors, Epigenetic Age, and Neurodevelopmental O
sentences: Story 3 is about Preterm Risk Factors, Epigenetic Age, and Neurodevelopmental Outcomes..
This is a recent research article from JAMA network open.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in children born at 24 to 32 weeks' gestation, recruited from 2 neonatal intensive care units from 2015 to 2019 and followed up to January 2026, how should we interpret Exposure or intervention stated in the title/objective. compared with Comparator or control group stated in the methods/results, if present.?
A total of 102 study participants (median gestational age, 27.0 weeks [IQR, 25.6-28.9 weeks]; 54 female [53%]) were included.
Higher maternal educational level (β = 11.65; 95% CI, 3.55-19.76; P = .005) and epigenetic age acceleration (β = 0.07; 95% CI, 0.01-0.14; P = .04) were associated with higher cognitive scores.

Epigenetic age acceleration was also associated with higher motor scores (β = 0.16; 95% CI, 0.06-0.27; P = .003), while extreme prematurity (β = -5.66; 95% CI, -10.85 to -0.46; P = .03) and severe brain injury (β = -10.99; 95% CI, -21.32 to -0.66; P = .04) were associated with lower motor scores.

script.heading: Outro
sentences: That wraps up today's journal club style update.
Before applying any finding, check the full source, the absolute effect size, and your local ICU context.

articles.title: Preterm Risk Factors, Epigenetic Age, and Neurodevelopmental Outcomes.
articles.summary: A total of 102 study participants (median gestational age, 27.0 weeks [IQR, 25.6-28.9 weeks]; 54 female [53%]) were included. Higher maternal educational level (β = 11.65; 95% CI, 3.55-19.76; P = .005) and epigenetic age acceleration (β = 0.07; 95% CI, 0.01-0.14; P = .04) were associated with higher cognitive scores. Epigenetic age acceleration was also associated with higher motor scores (β = 0.16; 95% CI, 0.06-0.27; P = .003), while extreme prematurity (β = -5.66; 95% CI, -10.85 to -0.46; P = .03) and severe brain injury (β = -10.99; 95% CI, -21.32 to -0.66; P = .04) were associated with lower motor scores. Severe brain injury modified the association between epigenetic aging and motor outcomes (β = 0.41; 95% CI, 0.08-0.74; P = .02), and children with epigenetic age acceleration in the presence of severe brain injury had higher motor scores. Studies examining biological factors associated with neurodevelopment in the preterm population are limited.
